guidance_facts.statement: The recommendation emphasizes that reducing total fat intake alone is not sufficient to prevent unhealthy weight gain.
Total fat intake should be at least 15–20% of total energy intake to ensure adequate energy and essential fatty acids.
The implementation of this recommendation must consider individual energy requirements and avoid excess energy intake.
In populations where undernutrition is a concern, maintaining or increasing total fat intake may be important to achieve adequate energy intake.
Reducing total fat intake can lead to a decrease in total energy intake, which may result in weight loss.
Infants should be exclusively breastfed for the first 6 months of life to achieve optimal growth, development, and health.
The guideline focuses on preventing unhealthy weight gain, not managing existing overweight or obesity.
Lower fat, restricted-calorie diets may be effective for short-term weight loss in individuals actively pursuing weight loss.
The recommendation emphasizes that reducing total fat intake alone is not sufficient to prevent unhealthy weight gain.
Total fat intake should be at least 15–20% of total energy intake to ensure adequate energy and essential fatty acids.
The implementation of this recommendation must consider individual energy requirements and avoid excess energy intake.
In populations where undernutrition is a concern, maintaining or increasing total fat intake may be important to achieve adequate energy intake.
All adults living with disability should undertake regular physical activity.

Adults living with disability should do at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity or an equivalent combination of moderate- and vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week.
Adults living with disability should also do muscle-strengthening activities at moderate or greater intensity that involve all major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week.

Older adults living with disability should do varied multicomponent physical activity that emphasizes functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity on 3 or more days a week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls.
Older adults should engage in at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity weekly.
Older adults should also perform muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week.
Varied multicomponent physical activity emphasizing functional balance and strength training should be done on 3 or more days a week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls.
Older adults may increase aerobic activity beyond 300 minutes of moderate-intensity or 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity for additional health benefits.
WHO recommends that adults limit total fat intake to 30% of total energy intake or less to reduce the risk of unhealthy weight gain.
This recommendation is specifically relevant for individuals aged 20 years or older.
The evidence was considered insufficient to support the formulation of a recommendation for children due to limited studies and inconsistent results.
For children aged 6 months and above and adolescents, total fat intakes of up to 35% of total energy are appropriate to meet growth demands without leading to excess energy intake.
The WHO guideline suggests that cardiovascular risk assessment should be conducted at or after the initiation of pharmacological treatment for hypertension.
Cardiovascular risk assessment is most important for guiding decisions about initiating pharmacological treatment for hypertension in those with lower SBP (130–139 mmHg).
CVD risk assessment is critical in those with HTN that other risk factors must be identified and treated appropriately to lower total cardiovascular risk.
In the absence of a calibrated equation for the local population, the choice of CVD risk-assessment systems should depend on resources available, acceptability, and feasibility of application.

The WHO recommends initiating pharmacological antihypertensive treatment for individuals with a confirmed diagnosis of hypertension and systolic blood pressure of ≥140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of ≥90 mmHg.
For individuals with existing cardiovascular disease, the WHO recommends pharmacological treatment if systolic blood pressure is 130–139 mmHg.

The WHO suggests pharmacological treatment for individuals without cardiovascular disease but with high cardiovascular risk, diabetes mellitus, or chronic kidney disease, and systolic blood pressure of 130–139 mmHg.
Pharmacological treatment for hypertension should start no later than four weeks following diagnosis, and earlier if blood pressure is very high or there is evidence of end organ damage.
Pharmacological treatment of hypertension can be provided by nonphysician professionals such as pharmacists and nurses.
Nonphysician professionals must have proper training, prescribing authority, specific management protocols, and physician oversight.
Community health care workers may assist in tasks such as education, delivery of medications, blood pressure measurement, and monitoring through a collaborative care model.
Telemonitoring and community or home-based self-care are encouraged to enhance blood pressure control as part of an integrated management system.

The recommendation to limit total fat intake to 30% of total energy intake is relevant for adults aged 20 years or older.
Physical activity is recommended for adults living with disability to enhance health benefits.
Physical activity is also recommended for older adults to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls.

The etiology of unhealthy weight gain is complex and involves multiple factors, not just total fat intake.
